records.body: Adopted in 1996, the coat of arms of Ethiopia features its national symbol, a pentagram. The blue circle symbolizes peace, and the pentagram represents the unity and equality of the Ethiopian people.
records.title: Ethiopia’s Coat of Arms

records.body: Today is the 250th birthday of celebrated English writer Jane Austen, who is known for her six classic novels depicting English middle-class life during the early 19th century. In 1817, Austen was buried in the Anglican Winchester Cathedral in Hampshire, England, which has the longest nave (pictured) of any Gothic cathedral in Europe. Founded in 1079, it is also famous for its seven chantry chapels, more than any other English cathedral.
records.title: Winchester Cathedral

records.body: The red crabs of Christmas Island live in deep burrows and rock crevices in the island’s rainforests. Once a year, during the rainy season, millions of the crabs migrate to the Indian Ocean to breed, covering the island in a blanket of red. On contact with the water, the crab larvae hatch and are swept out to sea. Those that survive emerge from the water as baby crabs and spend their first three years hidden in rocky outcrops.
records.title: Christmas Island’s Red Crabs

records.body: The unusual geological formation known as the Chocolate Hills in Bohol, Philippines, has almost 1,300 cone-shaped hills that are all about the same size, spread over about 50 sq km (19 sq mi). The grass on the hills turns brown during the dry season, giving the hills their name.
records.title: The “Chocolate” Hills

records.body: The Cook Islands coat of arms was designed by Papa Motu Kora, a mataiapo (traditional chief) from the Matavera village in Rarotonga. The shield with a circle of 15 five-pointed white stars represents the protection of the people and the country. Next to the shield are a flying fish (maroro) and a tern (kakaia). A Rarotongan orator club above the fish represents local traditions, and a cross above the tern symbolizes Christianity. A red-feathered Ariki headdress (pare kura) at the top of the shield represents the country’s traditional ranking system.
records.title: Cook Islands Coat of Arms

records.body: The poinsettia is native to Mexico and Central America. It has been associated with Christmas since the 17th century, when Franciscan friars in Mexico used it in holiday celebrations. In 1833, the poinsettia was named for avid botanist and first US Ambassador to Mexico Joel Roberts Poinsett, who propagated the plants at his home in South Carolina in the 1820s. Poinsettias became popular in the early 1900s and remain a popular Christmas decoration in homes, churches, and businesses across North America.
records.title: The Poinsettia

records.body: Antarctica (meaning “opposite to the Arctic”) is the world’s southernmost continent, as well as the driest, windiest, coldest, iciest, and highest continent. It is home to the emperor penguin (pictured), the largest of the 18 species of penguins at 120 cm (3.9 ft) tall. Emperor penguins are the world’s deepest-diving birds and can dive approximately 550 m (1,800 ft) in search of food. These penguins are found on ice shelves and land ice along the coast of Antarctica.
records.title: “Opposite to the Arctic”

records.body: The long-dormant Soufrière Hills volcano on the island of Montserrat stands 1,050 m (3,444 ft) tall and became active again in 1995, with its most recent eruption in 2013. A massive eruption in 1997 destroyed most of the capital, Plymouth, and rendered the southern part of the island uninhabitable. The government was moved to Brades Estate and other areas in the northwestern part of the island.
records.title: The Soufrière Hills volcano

records.body: Iceland’s coat of arms is derived from a 13th-century folktale about four guardians who protect the four corners of the nation. The bull protects the northwest, the eagle the northeast, the dragon the southeast, and the rock-giant the southwest. The shield displays the national flag, with red standing for Iceland’s volcanic fires, white for its snow and ice fields, and blue for the ocean.
records.title: Iceland’s Coat of Arms

records.body: The Christkindelsmärik (meaning "Market of the Christ Child" in the Alsatian dialect) is the oldest Christmas market in Europe, having been held annually in Strasbourg, France, since 1570. From November 29 to December 31 each year, Strasbourg becomes the "Capital of Christmas" for millions who visit the city.
records.title: The Christkindelsmärik

records.body: Native to the Australian territory of Norfolk Island, the Norfolk Island pine is a slow-growing species of conifer that reaches 60 m (200 ft) in its natural habitat, with a straight trunk measuring up to 3 m (10 ft) in diameter. This national symbol is found on the island’s coast and can tolerate high winds and sandy soil with high salt concentrations. The pines resemble Christmas trees and remain small when grown indoors, making them popular gifts during the holiday season. They are also in demand for use in woodturning, a decorative art that uses a lathe to carve wood.
records.title: The Norfolk Island Pine

records.body: St. Stephen’s Basilica is the third-largest church in Hungary and the largest church in Budapest. The church is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site that includes the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter, and Andrássy Avenue. Construction on this Catholic church, which is named for Hungary’s first king and patron saint Stephen I, began in the 1850s and was completed in 1905. At 96 m (315 ft), it is one of the two tallest buildings in Budapest.
records.title: St. Stephen’s Basilica

records.body: Faroese sheep are native to the Faroe Islands, an autonomous territory of Denmark. The name may derive from the old Norse word faer, meaning "sheep," and the Faroe Islands' coat of arms includes a silver ram, which is a national symbol. The sheep tend to have very little flocking instinct due to a lack of natural predators, and small groups range freely year-round. Sheep are a major part of the islands’ agricultural production.
records.title: The Sheep of Faroe Islands

records.body: The Heiliggeistkirche (Church of the Holy Spirit), constructed between 1398 and 1515, is the largest church in Heidelberg, Germany, and among the most visited churches in the country. Originally Roman Catholic, it changed denominations frequently over the centuries, and at one point, the nave and choir of the church were separated by a wall to allow Catholics and Protestants to worship at the same time. The wall was removed in 1936, and the church became solely Protestant.
records.title: The Heiliggeistkirche

records.body: Adopted in 1992, the coat of arms of Cabo Verde features the national symbol of ten stars that represent the country’s islands. The stylized torch and triangle at the center of the circle symbolize freedom and national unity, and the three blue lines represent the ocean and sky. The name of the country is written in Portuguese, the official language. The plumbob at the top of the circle -- used in construction to make accurate vertical lines -- represents justice, righteousness, and truth. The chain links symbolize a commitment to the people and their well-being.
records.title: Cabo Verde’s Coat of Arms

records.body: The Houses of Parliament building in Westminster, London, United Kingdom, is home to the famous Big Ben clock tower. Today the name refers to the tower, the clock, and the bell, but originally it applied solely to the tower’s largest bell, named for Sir Benjamin Hall, who oversaw the rebuilding of the Houses of Parliament after the 1834 fire. On New Year’s Eve in 1923, BBC Radio first broadcast Big Ben's chimes to the UK, and in 1932, the chimes were broadcast internationally as part of King George V’s Christmas address. In 2012, the structure was officially renamed the Elizabeth Tower in honor of Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee, but it is still widely referred to as "Big Ben."
records.title: Big Ben

records.body: Today is New Year’s Eve -- and National Champagne Day! The sparkling wine is a product of the Champagne region in northeastern France. Dom Pérignon, a French Benedictine monk who lived in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, made major improvements to the production and quality of champagne. A statue in his honor (pictured) stands outside the gate of the Abbey of Hautvillers in Epernay, where the monk lived. Moët & Chandon acquired the brand name Dom Pérignon in 1927.
records.title: National Champagne Day!
